title: First Kenyan-Born NFL Player Daniel Adongo Deported to Kenya by ICE
excerpt: The former Indianapolis Colts linebacker, who was twice found incompetent to stand trial and whose family says he suffers from a brain injury sustained while playing, was removed from the U.S. on June 20 after overstaying his visa for a decade.
body:
• Daniel Adongo, 37, the first Kenyan-born player in NFL history, was deported to Kenya on June 20 after a DOJ immigration judge ordered his removal in March.
  • ICE said Adongo overstayed his visa in 2016, a year after the Indianapolis Colts released him, and was held without bond under the Laken Riley Act.
  • Court records show judges twice found Adongo incompetent to stand trial; a psychiatrist raised the possibility of traumatic brain injury from his playing career.
  • His only conviction was a Class A misdemeanor for criminal mischief in 2020; felony charges against him were dismissed.

Daniel Adongo, the Nairobi-born rugby convert who became the first Kenyan to play in the NFL, has been deported to Kenya after a decade-long spiral through arrests, psychiatric hospitals, and immigration detention. U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement confirmed in a July 25 news release that Adongo, 37, was removed from the country on June 20.

A Department of Justice immigration judge ordered his removal on March 23, 2026. ICE said Adongo had overstayed his visa since 2016, one year after the Indianapolis Colts ended his contract. He was held without bond under the Laken Riley Act, the federal statute signed by President Trump in January 2025 that mandates detention of undocumented immigrants charged with certain offenses.

"This dangerous individual was clearly a threat to the community, which is now safer since he's been removed. Those who violate immigration law are held equally accountable, including former professional athletes."

— Douglas Thompson, ICE Chicago Assistant Field Office Director

From Super Rugby to the NFL

Adongo was 23 and playing Super Rugby in South Africa when Colts general manager Ryan Grigson signed him in July 2013. He had never watched a football game. The team spent a full season teaching him the sport on the practice field, according to the Indianapolis Star.

https://x.com/ICEgov/status/2082213309999096241

He appeared in five games over three seasons, played a single defensive snap, and earned roughly $694,000. Former teammate D'Qwell Jackson, an 11-year NFL veteran, told PEOPLE that Adongo was a dedicated player who embraced the challenge of learning a new sport from scratch.

"He was always a hard worker on the field and in the weight room. You didn't worry about him. He was everything in my opinion during that time that any coach or decision maker bringing in a guy like that would want. He was a model player."

— D'Qwell Jackson, former Colts teammate

Indianapolis waived Adongo in December 2015, a week after police were called to his home over a reported domestic disturbance — the second such call in two months. No charges were filed in either incident, according to ESPN.

Mental Health Questions and a Single Conviction

ICE said Adongo was arrested multiple times over the past nine years on charges including felony intimidation, battery, and disorderly conduct. But the felony charges were later dismissed. His sole conviction is a Class A misdemeanor for criminal mischief in 2020, for which he was sentenced to 364 days in jail.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=B7r8hlnKF98

Court records reviewed by the Indianapolis Star reveal a more complicated picture. Judges twice found Adongo incompetent to stand trial. In one filing, Dr. Jason Jaronik wrote that Adongo was acutely psychotic and raised the possibility of a traumatic brain injury from his playing days. In 2017, he spent time in a psychiatric facility after being deemed incompetent following a psychiatric examination, according to the Indy Star.

His mother, Betty Adongo, asked the court to release her son for a medical evaluation. Family members and social workers have said they believe his mental illness is tied to injuries sustained during his athletic career. The Indianapolis Star noted that no such link can be confirmed in a living patient.

A Case That Straddles Two Debates

Adongo's deportation sits at the intersection of two unresolved American conversations: the long-term neurological toll of contact sports and the expanding scope of immigration enforcement under the current administration. His case demonstrates how the Laken Riley Act functions in practice — an individual with a single misdemeanor conviction, dismissed felony charges, and documented psychiatric episodes was detained without bond and removed.

Jackson said he lost touch with Adongo after his release from the Colts. He told PEOPLE he didn't recognize the man in recent photographs.

"For someone to have it all and then it goes sideways, it raises my suspicions that there are some mental issues that could be possibly going on," Jackson said. "I wish things could have worked out better for him because the person I know is a good person."

What's Next

Adongo is now back in Kenya, though his medical situation remains unclear. The Colts did not respond to PEOPLE's request for comment. Whether Adongo's family will pursue medical treatment for a possible brain injury in Kenya — where resources for TBI diagnosis and care are far more limited — is an open question. For immigrant athletes whose careers end abruptly, his case underscores the risks of falling through gaps in both the healthcare and immigration systems.
nri_angle: Adongo's case highlights the precarious immigration status many foreign-born athletes face when careers in the U.S. end abruptly, leaving them without visa sponsorship and vulnerable to enforcement actions years later.
author: Diaspora Desk
